records.title: YouTuber arrested five times in a week after a speech criticising the Deputy Chief Minister; anti-terror law added
records.authority: Andhra Pradesh Police (several districts); remanded by a court at Gannavaram
laws: Sections 13 and 39, Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967

records.person: A Dalit Christian YouTuber and activist
records.summary: A YouTuber who criticised Deputy Chief Minister Pawan Kalyan at a Dalit Christian meeting in Eluru on 28 June 2026 was arrested five times in about a week by police in different districts, each time in a new case after the last one ended in bail or a refused remand. The fifth case, over a video posted in November 2025, added the anti-terror law UAPA, and a court remanded him to judicial custody until 18 July.
detail: News reports say the YouTuber spoke at a Dalit Christian meeting in Eluru in late June 2026, where he attacked ruling-party leaders over what he called inaction on atrocities against Dalits. IANS reported the date as 28 June and said the complaint concerned 'derogatory remarks' against Deputy Chief Minister Pawan Kalyan.

According to ThePrint, he was first taken into custody on 30 June by Kakinada district police. After bail he was arrested again on 2 July by Sarpavaram police in a pending 2025 case, then on 3 July by Machilipatnam and Inaguduru police, and on 4 July by Payakaraopeta police, when a court at Anakapalli rejected the remand request. IANS reported that he 'secured bail for the fourth time on July 4'.

He was then arrested a fifth time by Gannavaram police in Krishna district at the Vempadu toll plaza. Police invoked sections 13 and 39 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act and several sections of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, including section 152 (acts endangering the sovereignty and integrity of India). ThePrint reported that police said a video he posted on 25 November 2025 was 'very provocative' and 'supported and encouraged banned organisations such as the Maoists', and that it showed pictures of Maoist leaders killed in encounters.

A court at Gannavaram remanded him to judicial custody until 18 July 2026, and he was lodged in Nellore Central Jail, according to the same reports. His wife told reporters that he 'spoke the very same language that Pawan Kalyan used'.

On 17 September 2026 a court at Gannavaram granted Gannavaram police seven days' custody of him in the UAPA case, Deccan Chronicle reported. Police said they wanted to question him about the network behind his videos, alleged links with former IAS and IPS officers, and political motives, and alleged that remarks at the Eluru meeting could encourage youngsters towards Naxalism.
records.current_position: In police custody in the UAPA case from 18 September 2026 for seven days, per Deccan Chronicle; the prosecutions are pending.

sections.label: Why it is listed
sections.heading: Speech, then a stack of cases
sections.text: The first arrest followed a political speech criticising a minister. The pattern that followed, a fresh arrest in a different district each time a court released him, ending in an anti-terror charge over a months-old video, is the kind of use of criminal process against speech this register documents. The courts have made no finding on the charges.

records.caveats: No court order in these cases has been published online yet, so this record rests on news reports (V1). Reports differ on whether the fifth arrest was on 4 or 5 July 2026. We do not know whether he has since been granted bail in the UAPA case.

records.title: Pastor loses Scheduled Caste status for practising Christianity; his caste certificates are cancelled
records.authority: Supreme Court of India; District Collector, Bapatla
records.case_reference: Criminal Appeal No. 1580 of 2026, 2026 INSC 283 (from Crl.P. No. 7114 of 2022, High Court of Andhra Pradesh; FIR No. 08 of 2021, Chandole Police Station)
laws: Paragraph 3, Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order, 1950

acts: Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989

records.person: A pastor from Kothapalem village, Bapatla district
records.summary: A Dalit pastor who said he was assaulted and warned to stop holding Sunday prayer meetings lost the protection of the anti-atrocities law because he practises Christianity. On 24 March 2026 the Supreme Court held that conversion ends Scheduled Caste status 'from the moment of conversion'. On 23 May 2026 the Bapatla district collector cancelled his three caste certificates.
detail: The Supreme Court recorded that the appellant, from Kothapalem village in Pittalavanipalem mandal, belongs by birth to the Madiga community, a Scheduled Caste, and had for about ten years been conducting Sunday prayer meetings as a pastor in houses in the village.

He alleged that in January 2021 men from the village assaulted him, abused him by caste and 'warned him against continuing the prayer meetings'. Chandole police registered FIR No. 08 of 2021 under the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act and the Indian Penal Code and filed a charge sheet.

On 30 April 2025 the High Court of Andhra Pradesh quashed the case, holding that a person who 'had been openly professing Christianity and working as a Pastor' cannot claim protection under the SC/ST Act. On 24 March 2026 a Supreme Court bench of Justices Prashant Kumar Mishra and Manmohan dismissed his appeal. It held that under paragraph 3 of the Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order, 1950, only Hindus, Sikhs and Buddhists can be members of a Scheduled Caste, and that no statutory benefit or protection tied to caste status can be extended to anyone else.

News reports say that after the ruling a District Level Scrutiny Committee enquired into his caste status, and that on its recommendation the Bapatla District Collector cancelled three certificates issued to him (dated 15 March 2021, 22 October 2022 and 28 February 2025) with immediate effect, by an Extraordinary Gazette notification dated 23 May 2026.

The Supreme Court also agreed with the High Court that the investigation material did not support the assault and intimidation allegations. This record takes no view on those allegations; it concerns the holding that his religion alone removes his caste status.
records.current_position: Scheduled Caste status held lost by the Supreme Court (24 March 2026); caste certificates cancelled by the Bapatla district collector (gazette of 23 May 2026, as reported).

quote.heading: What the Supreme Court held
quote.text: No person who professes a religion other than Hindu, Sikh or Buddhist shall be deemed to be a member of a Scheduled Caste. This bar under Clause 3 of the Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order, 1950 is categorical and absolute. Conversion to any religion not specified in Clause 3 results in immediate and complete loss of Scheduled Caste status from the moment of conversion regardless of birth.
quote.where: Supreme Court of India, 2026 INSC 283 (Criminal Appeal No. 1580 of 2026), conclusions (b)

sections.label: Why it is listed
sections.heading: A status that depends on faith
sections.text: A Hindu, Sikh or Buddhist of the same caste keeps Scheduled Caste status and the legal protections that go with it; a Christian or Muslim loses them. The pastor's certificates were cancelled because of the religion he practises, which makes this a penalty on professing a faith.

records.caveats: We have not located the 23 May 2026 gazette notification online; its details come from news reports that quote it. The Supreme Court judgment is the primary record.

records.summary: A senior journalist working for a digital news portal was prosecuted in a criminal defamation case over a November 2019 investigative report on land dealings near the China border. The complaint was filed by a former advisor to the chief minister. On 25 June 2025 the Court of the Judicial Magistrate First Class, Namsai, dismissed the complaint for non-prosecution and acquitted the journalist.

The Arunachal Observer recorded that the complaint was filed by a former advisor to the chief minister. EastMojo reported that after the article the journalist received telephonic threats and that the state's press bodies condemned the intimidation as an attack on journalistic freedom.

The Arunachal Observer recorded that the case came before the Judicial Magistrate First Class, Namsai. The Sentinel reported: "Judicial Magistrate First Class [name withheld], while passing the order on June 25, cited Section 256 of the CrPC, which empowers courts to dismiss cases for non-prosecution."

The same report noted that the complainant and his counsel were absent despite a final opportunity granted on payment of Rs 2,000 in costs. EastMojo reported that the journalist said a bailable arrest warrant had been issued against her during the case and that she had travelled repeatedly from Itanagar to Namsai for hearings.
records.current_position: The complaint was dismissed for non-prosecution and the journalist stands cleared of the allegations; the case is closed.

records.summary: Police in Jamnagar registered an FIR against a Rajya Sabha member over a video with a poem posted on X. The Gujarat High Court refused to quash it in January 2025. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal on 28 March 2025 and quashed the FIR and all further proceedings.

The Karnataka High Court quashed the FIR on 11 September 2026. It held a WhatsApp status seen by one's contacts is not publication or circulation, and showed no intent to cause disorder.
records.date_label: High Court order quashing the FIR
records.authority: Karnataka High Court, Justice Rajesh Rai K; Subramanya Police Station
records.case_reference: Criminal Petition No. 5909 of 2024; Crime No. 38/2024
laws: Section 505(2) of the Indian Penal Code, 1860
records.person: a 49-year-old resident of Sullia taluk
detail: The High Court recorded that a Congress party worker complained on 07.06.2024 that the man's WhatsApp status on 05.06.2024 about the election result created enmity between communities, and that Subramanya Police registered Crime No. 38/2024 under Section 505(2) IPC.
The High Court held that a careful reading of the status disclosed no intention or motive to cause disorder or incite people to violence.
The High Court held that a WhatsApp status is not a public forum and is normally visible only to people in the user's contact list, so the ingredient of publication or circulation was absent.
The High Court held that continuing the case was an abuse of process and quashed the FIR.
records.current_position: The FIR in Crime No. 38/2024 stands quashed.
